title: Sense Giving, Clarity, Not Certainty
author: Nick Hart
summary: Hart's short argument turns on a distinction leaders routinely collapse: clarity and certainty are not the same thing. Certainty belongs to mechanical systems with predictable inputs and outputs, while schools are ecosystems in which relationships, emotions and feedback loops determine what happens next. He suggests the pull toward certainty is self-protective, shielding leaders from the vulnerability of not knowing, while actually amplifying the anxiety of staff who can see the gap between the official narrative and lived reality. Sense giving is then defined as helping others interpret complexity without pretending to eliminate it, and Hart insists it can be done either directively or relationally. The danger lies not in a command and control style but in any style that shades into false certainty. He carves out explicit exceptions where directive clarity is right, naming safeguarding, crisis moments and non-negotiable ethical boundaries. Three practices follow: point out the direction, name the unknowns, and stay present so people can see you thinking aloud. The closing section identifies the hardest part as emotional discipline, the steadiness required to hold ambiguity without letting it leak as anxiety.
points: The three-line contrast is the piece's most portable tool: certainty imposes a fixed narrative, tells people what to think and withholds ambiguity, while clarity frames shared sense making, invites co-construction and embraces ambiguity.
Hart refuses the easy binary that relational leadership is always superior, arguing instead that both directive and relational approaches can deliver clarity and both can curdle into certainty.
Naming the unknowns is defended on the grounds that unspoken ambiguity converts into anxiety, so saying what is not yet known is a form of reassurance rather than weakness.
The observation that leaders who rush to sound decisive may be managing their own discomfort rather than their team's is the sharpest diagnostic line in the piece.
Safeguarding, emergencies and ethical boundaries are flagged as domains where discussion is the wrong instinct and decisive coordination prevents harm, with the relational work belonging to recovery.
quotes: We seek certainty because it’s comforting. It feels safe to believe that good leadership means knowing what comes next whether we believe it of ourselves or others.

In a complex adaptive system, relationships, emotions and feedback loops shape what happens next. The seductive thing about certainty is that it protects us from vulnerability, hiding our own discomfort with not knowing. Yet pretending to know only amplifies the anxiety of those who are making sense of the gap between the narrative and the reality.
This is where sense giving comes in, the art of helping others interpret complexity without pretending to eliminate it.
Certainty imposes a fixed narrative while clarity offers a framework for shared sense making.
Ambiguity unspoken becomes anxiety. Say what you don’t yet know and how you’re working on it.
The hardest part of attempting to offer clarity is resisting the urge to sound certain.

Leaders who rush to sound decisive might be doing so to manage their own discomfort, not their team’s. But those who stay honest about uncertainty model something more valuable, confidence and humility.
